arguments.claim: The Court reiterates that a person charged with a criminal offence is entitled to take part in the hearing and to defend himself in person or through legal assistance.

anchor.surface_text: The Court reiterates that the object and purpose of Article 6 of the Convention, taken as a whole, implies that a person charged with a criminal offence is entitled to take part in the hearing. Moreover, sub-paragraph (c) of paragraph 3 guarantees to “everyone charged with a criminal offence” the right “to defend himself in person” and it is difficult to see how these rights could be exercised without the person concerned being present at the actual trial.

arguments.claim: The applicants were not invited to attend the hearings before the Ni1fde Criminal Court which sentenced them to four years' imprisonment.

anchor.surface_text: The Court observes that in the instant case the applicants were not invited to attend the hearings before the Ni1fde Criminal Court which sentenced them to four years' imprisonment.

arguments.claim: The fact that the applicants raised no objections when the Bandirma Criminal Court took their statements does not signify that they implicitly waived their right to defend themselves or to appear before the Ni1fde Criminal Court, since waiver must be unequivocal.

anchor.surface_text: The Court finds that, contrary to the Government's contention, the fact that the applicants raised no objections when the Bandirma Criminal Court took their statements does not signify that they implicitly waived their right to defend themselves or to appear before the Ni1fde Criminal Court, since the waiver of the exercise of a right guaranteed by the Convention must be established in an unequivocal manner.

arguments.court_reasoning: The Court accepted the applicants' claim based on lawyers' failure to attend hearings and lack of court intervention.

arguments.claim: The appointment of defence counsel does not necessarily ensure effective assistance; the State must intervene if legal aid counsel fails manifestly to provide effective representation.

anchor.surface_text: The Court reiterates that the appointment of defence counsel in itself does not necessarily settle the issue of compliance with the requirements of Article 6 �� 3 (c). The Convention is intended to guarantee not rights which are theoretical or illusory, but rights which are practical and effective. Thus, mere nomination does not ensure effective assistance since a lawyer appointed for legal aid purposes may be prevented from performing, or shirk his or her duties. If they are notified of the situation, the authorities must either replace or oblige the lawyer to fulfil those duties.

arguments.claim: The conduct of the defence is essentially a matter between the defendant and his counsel; the State is required to intervene only if failure by legal aid counsel is manifest or sufficiently brought to attention.

anchor.surface_text: Nevertheless, a State cannot be held responsible for every shortcoming of a lawyer appointed for legal aid purposes. It follows from the independence of the legal profession that the conduct of the defence is essentially a matter between the defendant and his counsel, whether counsel be appointed under a legal aid scheme or be privately financed. The Court considers that the competent national authorities are required under Article 6 �� 3 (c) to intervene only if a failure by legal aid counsel to provide effective representation is manifest or sufficiently brought to their attention in some other way.

arguments.claim: The Ni1fde Bar Association appointed two lawyers on 29 May 2000 to assist the applicants, but the lawyers did not attend any of the six hearings held by the Ni1fde Criminal Court.

anchor.surface_text: Turning to the circumstances of the present case, the Court notes that, upon the request of the Ni1fde Criminal Court, the Ni1fde Bar Association appointed two lawyers on 29 May 2000 to assist the applicants with their case (paragraph 13 above). The Court observes from the minutes of the six hearings held by the Ni1fde Criminal Court that the lawyers did not attend any of them.

arguments.claim: The Ni1fde Criminal Court must have been aware of the lawyers' failure to fulfil their obligations but did not take any measures to ensure compliance.

anchor.surface_text: It therefore considers that the Ni1fde Criminal Court must have been aware of the lawyers' failure to fulfil their obligations. The Court further notes that the domestic court did not take any measures to ensure that the lawyers comply with their duties.

arguments.claim: The proceedings before the Ni1fde Criminal Court did not comply with the requirement of fairness, constituting a breach of Article 6 §§ 1 and 3(c) of the Convention.

anchor.surface_text: The foregoing considerations are sufficient to enable the Court to conclude that the proceedings before the Ni1fde Criminal Court did not comply with the requirement of fairness. There has consequently been a breach of Article 6 �� 1 and 3(c) of the Convention.
